scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The parai is one of the ancient native percussion instruments developed by the Tamil people, with its name deriving from the Tamil verb meaning 'to speak' or 'to tell'.

Early references appear in Sangam literature, including the Kuṟuntokai, which describes the drum being played during auspicious occasions, while announcers who delivered messages were termed Paraiyar.
The instrument is also documented in the Tirumurai, a twelve-volume compendium of devotional hymns dating between the 6th and 11th centuries CE.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Historically used as a communication tool, the parai gathered communities, alerted people to warfare, proclaimed victory or defeat, signaled reservoir breaches, summoned farm laborers, and frightened away wild animals.
In devotional settings, it is played in Hindu temple processions for deities and in the worship of traditional Tamil guardian deities such as Muneeswarar.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: In Parai Attam, the musician is simultaneously the dancer.
The drum is slung across one shoulder using a cloth strap called a nadai, allowing the performer to dance while standing, walking, or seated with the drum on the lap.
Performers execute rhythmic patterns resembling classical dance movements, swaying their bodies and stamping their feet in tight synchronization with their own drumming.
Watch for Adi Kucchi Center Strike, Sundu Kuchi Slap, Synchronized Stamping and Sway.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is driven entirely by the parai, a shallow circular wooden frame drum measuring 16 to 22 inches in diameter, typically crafted from hardwoods like jackfruit tree wood.
A single animal hide is stretched over the frame, tightened using leather straps, ropes, glue, and nails.
Listen for the Parai (frame drum), Adi Kucchi (short thick wooden stick), Sundu Kuchi (long bamboo stick), Tharai (woodwind horn).

A sharp, explosive, high-pitched percussion sound produced by a fire-tempered animal hide frame drum beaten rapidly with a combination of a stubby wooden mallet and a flexible bamboo stick, punctuated by the shrill calls of the tharai woodwind.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performances take place in open communal spaces, streets, temple compounds, and festival stages.
The instrument is slung over the shoulder with a cloth harness known as a nadai, leaving both hands free to strike the drum while maneuvering through outdoor processions or arena formats.
Setting the instrument involves preparing a small bonfire in the performance area to warm and tension the drumheads prior to play.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Tamil film director Bala brought the art form into mainstream cinema with his 2016 film Tharai Thappattai.
The soundtrack, scored by composer Ilaiyaraaja, featured traditional parai instrumentation prominently.
Regional forms and drum variations reflect diverse functional and geographical adaptations.

visual_brief.setting_notes: Historically used as a communication tool, the parai gathered communities, alerted people to warfare, proclaimed victory or defeat, signaled reservoir breaches, summoned farm laborers, and frightened away wild animals. In devotional settings, it is played in Hindu temple processions for deities and in the worship of traditional Tamil guardian deities such as Muneeswarar.
